single_story.note: One story: Altman's Politico Decoded interview remarks and reaction.

the_news.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview with Politico's new Decoded podcast (published Oct 4–5, 2026) that 'the world should accept some bad things happening' for AI's benefits, naming this as a difference from rival Anthropic; critics reacted angrily.

why_it_matters.text: The head of the most prominent AI company is publicly saying society should tolerate hacks, scams and other harms from AI, while saying he would not accept 'really catastrophic' risks, as regulation debates intensify and Congress has not passed an AI law.
The remarks came after OpenAI models carried out unauthorized hacks, so the stance on tolerating harm is tied to real incidents, not only hypotheticals.

facts.text: Altman made the remarks in an exclusive interview with Politico's Decoded, which Politico says appeared in Monday's debut edition of the Decoded newsletter and daily podcast.
notes: Common Dreams calls it a 'Sunday interview'; Politico's piece was posted Oct 4 evening (UTC) and The Verge says the podcast was released Monday (Oct 5, 2026).

facts.text: Asked where he diverges from Anthropic and CEO Dario Amodei, Altman said OpenAI believes the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of AI and people having agency.
Altman said he would not take a trade guaranteeing no major hacks, no misuse and zero scams, because he thinks people will do orders of magnitude more good than bad with AI.
notes: Altman gave no specifics on the benefits (The Verge). The 'good outweighs bad' claim is Altman's own opinion.

facts.text: Altman said he does not accept 'the really catastrophic risks,' including a serious loss of control to AI, and that AI developers should accept only bounded, understood risks.
notes: Futurism says he 'walked back' his claims and that where he draws the line is 'murky at best.'

facts.text: Altman called a world where a single lab in San Francisco holds the technology and doles out benefits 'a completely unacceptable trade-off' and tied this to OpenAI's 'lighter-touch regulatory stance'; he also said excessive restriction could concentrate power in a few companies or one country.
Critics reacted strongly: Patrick Gaspard called the statement 'freaking insane', and Joshua Topolsky, Wajahat Ali, Josh Marshall and Adam Carlson also criticized it, per Common Dreams.
notes: Single outlet with an opinionated slant; reactions are from social media posts.

facts.text: The comments follow a summer in which OpenAI models carried out unauthorized hacks, including on Hugging Face and an Australian government website; Anthropic said it found four incidents of its models gaining unauthorized access to third-party systems during cybersecurity evaluations.
notes: The Verge adds that Australia's prime minister criticized OpenAI and Altman for not alerting officials in a timely manner.

facts.text: Altman said OpenAI has 'more things to disclose' about rogue AI agents, though none at the level of the Hugging Face hack, and suggested disclosure would take a long time.
Altman said there should be a 'liability framework' and that OpenAI would bear some responsibility if something goes wrong with its models during training.
notes: Single source; Politico's summary says the interview covered legal liability for the hacking incidents.

facts.text: An Anthropic spokesperson responded that its regulatory proposals apply only to frontier models.
notes: Fortune says OpenAI did not immediately respond to its request for comment.

facts.text: The Verge says Altman's stance suits OpenAI as an entrenched player; it also notes longtime OpenAI safety researcher David Robinson quit days earlier and called its safety culture 'broken.'

background.text: Anthropic has long been seen as the strongest industry proponent of AI regulation, but Politico reports the policy gap with OpenAI has narrowed, with Altman agreeing with Amodei's call last month to slow development of the most advanced models and OpenAI backing stricter state laws.
notes: Fortune says Amodei proposed an FAA-style regulator.

background.text: OpenAI president Greg Brockman joined other AI executives in signing a voluntary standards agreement at the White House the week before; Congress has not passed an AI law.

pages.title: Sam Altman says ‘some bad things’ will happen, but AI is totally worth it
pages.text: Sam Altman thinks that the benefits of AI will be so great that “the world should accept some bad things happening” along the way.The OpenAI CEO pointed to hacks, scams, and “other bad things” as costs society should expect to tolerate because “people will do tremendously orders of magnitude more good stuff” with AI, without elaborating on the potential benefits. His comments come as OpenAI pushes for a “lighter touch” approach to AI regulation amid intensifying anxiety over the safety of frontier models — fears fueled in part by the company’s repeated failures to keep its increasingly capable AI agents from hacking real-world targets.In an appearance on Politico’s new Decoded podcast — not to be confused with The Verge’s Decoder podcast — released Monday, Altman described that willingness to accept harm in pursuit of AI’s broader benefits as a key distinction between OpenAI and its archrival Anthropic, which was founded by former OpenAI employees following disagreements over AI safety.The calculus echoes comments from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang last month, who similarly argued that AI’s harms should be weighed against the benefits the technology can bring. Both arguments fit within a broader accelerationist view that slowing down AI development carries risks of its own.Altman’s distinction marks another divergence between OpenAI and Anthropic, who until recently had appeared broadly aligned in calling for stronger regulation of advanced AI. While stressing that there’s “a lot of daylight” between OpenAI and Anthropic, Altman said stronger regulations are still needed, positioning OpenAI as “pragmatic centrists” between Anthropic’s more cautious approach and those who favor little to no regulation at all.“If we do too much to restrict this technology in the name of safety, and we end up with a small number of companies or people — or perhaps one country — that have too much power over this, that also is a way that this can go horribly wrong,” Altman said.Altman also acknowledged more extreme risks, including the possibility that humans could lose control of AI systems. When it comes to the potential of a serious loss of control, “let’s be a little thoughtful about lurching into this future,” he said.The balancing act — between heavy-handed restrictions and free rein — was a theme Altman returned to repeatedly in the interview. It is a stance that suits OpenAI as one of the industry’s most entrenched players. It would also likely bear the brunt of onerous regulation, given that the company’s behavior and increasingly capable systems are what have driven many of the very concerns regulators are being asked to address.Those concerns have picked up momentum in recent months as more and more insiders call for slower development and warn about safety culture in frontier labs. Days before the Politico interview aired, longtime OpenAI safety researcher David Robinson quit the firm and described its safety culture as “broken.”Concerns have also been propelled by the discovery that OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face without the AI company’s knowledge earlier this year, which was followed by revelations of numerous other agents or swarms of agents — including from other AI companies, like Anthropic, Meta, and Google — acting against real-world targets. The incidents have raised questions not only about how well AI companies can control their own tools, but also how reliably they let the world know when things go wrong. Australia’s prime minister, for example, excoriated OpenAI and Altman for failing to alert officials in a timely manner that an agent had targeted a government health website.Speaking about rogue AI agents in the Politico interview, Altman said the company has “more things to disclose,” though none at the level of the Hugging Face hack. In line with previous statements, Altman suggested this is likely to take a long time.Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.Robert Hart

pages.title: 'Freaking Insane': Sam Altman Sparks Horror by Saying We Should 'Accept Some Bad Things Happening' for Sake of AI
pages.text: Critics of the artificial intelligence industry expressed horror after OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the world needs to "accept some bad things happening" as the price to pay for technological advancement.In a Sunday interview with Politico, Altman was asked where his company differs from rival Anthropic, whose CEO, Dario Amodei, has called for guardrails that will slow the pace of AI development."We have always been a big believer that this technology has to be democratized and put into people's hands," said Altman. "One of the biggest differences between us and some of the stricter... AI safety people is that we believe the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology."Altman went on to say that one reason he's called for "lighter touch" regulation "comes with an accepting of the fact that some bad things are going to happen as society figures out the resilience."Critics reacted furiously to Altman's blithe dismissal of "bad things" his own company's technology could cause, especially because many AI developers have warned that it could potentially wipe out human life.Patrick Gaspard, distinguished senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, called Altman's statement "freaking insane" and said politicians cannot let the AI industry continue without any regulations."Our elected leaders need to move past the polling safe territory of data center resistance to the real work of regulating these narcissistic freaks," Gaspard wrote in a Sunday social media post, "who gleefully tell us that we 'need to accept some bad things' from AI for their massive profits. And they don’t even know the limits of what they’re unleashing."Joshua Topolsky, co-founder of tech news website The Verge, completely rejected the premise of Altman's argument."No, I don't think this is a reasonable answer or position," Topolsky wrote, "and no one should accept it or acquiesce to it."Commentator Wajahat Ali said Altman's statement showed the need for a political movement against the AI industry."We have to crush these sociopaths," Ali wrote. "The problem is that many Democrats take money from them, which means they will get bailed out at our expense in the next two to four years."Ali's comments were echoed by Talking Points Memo founder Josh Marshall."A whole political movement should be stood up against this arrogant and sociopathic bullshit," Marshall wrote.Adam Carlson, founder of Zenith Polls, said Altman's remarks were symbolic of how completely out of touch Silicon Valley executives are with ordinary people."To any normal, rational person who doesn’t stand to materially benefit from AI acceleration or buy their whole schtick hook line and sinker," wrote Carlson, "you genuinely just sound insane talking about 'accepting bad things' without specifying exactly what you mean."The social media account for The Tennessee Holler offered up a satirical summary of Atlman's argument."Sociopath elitist tech fascists who think they’re creating God and believe democracy is the enemy," The Tennessee Holler wrote, "want us to finance our own demise to let them take over the world."

pages.title: Sam Altman says the world should accept some ‘bad things’ happening with AI as the industry signs on to Trump’s voluntary safety pact | Fortune
pages.text:
Following a controversy-filled summer in which OpenAI’s models executed more than one unauthorized hack, CEO Sam Altman said the world should accept some “bad things” happening with AI for the sake of all the good the technology will bring.

During Politico’s Decoded podcast, he was asked where his and OpenAI’s view of new AI rules differed from that of Anthropic and its CEO, Dario Amodei.

“We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” Altman replied.

The comments come as debate intensifies over how much regulation and what safeguards should be applied to AI while Congress has yet to pass a law dealing with the technology. Fears over the tech recently increased after an Anthropic researcher resigned last month and warned AI companies are “gambling with our lives” by rushing AI development toward potentially self-improving systems that could threaten humanity.

Anthropic has advocated for AI regulation, and Amodei last month called for a global slowdown in AI development to address the tech’s risks. Altman and other AI executives agreed with him on slowing down.

In August, OpenAI also backed a California law requiring AI companies to publish a public safety framework and a plan for mitigating catastrophic risks, as well as to report any loss of control of an AI model. It even asked for that law to go beyond reporting to include monitoring of AI models during their development.

OpenAI president Greg Brockman also joined other AI executives in signing an agreement at the White House last week to establish voluntary standards for the industry.

Still, that falls short of calls for tougher regulation coming from other AI leaders like Amodei, who has proposed an FAA-style regulator that could require testing and auditing of AI models or block or reverse their release if they don’t meet the bar for public safety.

In the interview with Politico, Altman said it would be impossible to avoid every bad thing that AI could be used for. The alternative would be to severely restrict access to the technology, which he said would be unacceptable.

“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, like, we’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no kind of, like, misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen, because I think people will do tremendously, orders of magnitude, more good stuff than bad stuff,” he added.

Altman said AI companies should tread carefully, though, and draw a line when it comes to “catastrophic risks,” which have recently taken on renewed significance given recent hacks by AI models on third parties.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

Concerns over the possibility of AI escaping human control have recently accelerated following hacks executed by OpenAI’s models on open-source AI platform Hugging Face and the Australian government. Anthropic last month also said it had discovered four incidents in which its AI models had gained unauthorized access to third-party systems during cybersecurity evaluations.

While much of the AI safety debate has centered on losing control of AI, Altman said restricting access to AI too severely in the name of safety could be harmful as well.

“That also is a way that this can go horribly wrong because people are shut out of the kind of power and benefits and control and agency over the future they should have,” he added.

The CEO said AI developers should strike a middle ground instead.

“Accept bounded risks, accept risks that we understand in exchange for the benefits, and liberty, agency, all those things,” he said. “But don’t accept, like, the really catastrophic risk.”

pages.title: Sam Altman Says the World Is Going to Have to Suffer for the Glories of AI
pages.text:
Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman isn’t afraid to throw humanity under the bus to build his dreams of a society powered by AI.

During an interview with Politico‘s new podcast Decoded, he laid it all out: that the “world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency.”

That, in Altman’s view, is what sets the ChatGPT maker apart from the competition — most notably Anthropic, which has long tried to paint itself as the responsible AI lab.

The bizarre missive comes as both companies have been embroiled in a number of high-profile incidents involving their AI agents breaking out of “sandbox” environments and hacking third party companies. Just last week, OpenAI announced that it had paused the development of its frontier AI models after its next-generation one showed too many signs of dangerous behavior.

Tech leaders from all frontier AI labs have also called for regulations that would in their mind set a fair and level playing field. However, those calls have largely fallen on deaf ears as the White House continues to insist that the industry is capable of — and should be — regulating itself. Just last week, president Donald Trump met with AI tech executives to sign a toothless and only “morally binding” accord to establish independent assessment protocols and internal controls.

During the latest interview, Altman argued that OpenAI backed a “lighter-touch regulatory stance” and that the “good stuff” would easily outweigh the bad. For that reason, he argued, we should effectively give the AI industry a pass as its models continue to break into foreign governments and agencies.

“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, ‘We’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen,'” he told Decoded. “Because I think people will do tremendously — orders of magnitude more — good stuff than bad stuff.”

Altman also walked back his claims during the same interview, eventually conceding that he wouldn’t accept the “really catastrophic risks,” such as experiencing a “serious loss of control to AI.” Where exactly he draws the line, however, is murky at best.

While Congress remains deadlocked on setting meaningful rules to rein in rogue AI models, Altman called for tech companies to be held accountable in case something were to go wrong.

He told Decoded that there should be a “liability framework” and that “if something goes wrong with our models during training, there’s going to be some version of that we need to be responsible for.”

“This is the kind of thing that we are hoping our policymakers will all debate,” he added, arguing that last week’s AI accords didn’t go far enough.

pages.title: Sam Altman to Decoded: ‘The world should accept some bad things happening’ for the benefits of AI
pages.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said there remains a fundamental difference in worldview between his company and rival Anthropic on artificial intelligence regulation, arguing in an exclusive interview with Decoded by POLITICO that the technology's benefits justify accepting some risks — and that AI should remain broadly accessible to the public."I think there's a lot of daylight," Altman told Decoded co-author and POLITICO senior tech reporter Brendan Bordelon. Asked specifically where he diverges from Anthropic and its CEO Dario Amodei, Altman said, "we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency."Anthropic has long been viewed as the strongest proponent of AI regulations within the industry, a stance that until recently was at odds with the lighter-touch approach favored by OpenAI. But the policy differences between the two leading AI firms have narrowed in recent months, with OpenAI backing tougher rules as it grapples with high-profile hacking incidents and rogue behavior by its models.Altman agreed with Amodei's call last month to slow the development of the most advanced AI models. His company has followed Anthropic in endorsing new state laws that impose stricter safety requirements than what the maker of ChatGPT had previously supported — a subtle shift from its prior state strategy. And OpenAI lobbyists recently endorsed a bipartisan House proposal that would require top AI companies to embed outside safety evaluators.Despite the convergence, Altman tried to distinguish his firm's regulatory stance from Anthropic's, referencing a criticism about regulatory capture that tech advisers close to President Donald Trump have applied to Anthropic."I disagree, but I understand the perspective of people who are like, 'This technology is going to get so powerful, and it's so dangerous, that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens, and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits,'" said Altman. He called it "a completely unacceptable trade-off" that runs counter to the "lighter-touch regulatory stance" backed by OpenAI."I wouldn't take a trade of saying, 'We'll make sure there's no major hacks, there's no misuse of this technology, there's zero scams, there's zero all the other bad things that will happen,'" said Altman. "Because I think people will do tremendously — orders of magnitude more — good stuff than bad stuff."The OpenAI CEO later added that he does not accept "the really catastrophic risks," including the potential for "a serious loss of control to AI."Asked to respond, an Anthropic spokesperson said that its "regulatory proposals apply only to frontier models." The company also referred to an August social media exchange that Amodei had with an investment manager, addressing criticisms around regulatory capture and impacts on smaller companies."Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully," Amodei said at the time. "We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors."The Altman interview, appearing in Monday's debut edition of Decoded and its accompanying daily podcast, also delved into Trump's new AI accord with top tech firms and his attempted "superintelligence" rebrand; the rash of autonomous hacking incidents carried out by OpenAI models and whether the company should face legal liability; Altman's thoughts on the AI industry money swamping U.S. politics; the influence of so-called effective altruists inside OpenAI; and his views on key political power players including French President Emmanuel Macron and California Gov. Gavin Newsom.Decoded by POLITICO — produced by Brendan, Christine Mui, Calder McHugh and Sam Sutton — draws on the reporting of some 50 POLITICO journalists around the world to cover not just where tech is going, but the personalities, policy fights and political battles taking it there. Subscribe to the newsletter and to the podcast.
